title: The Limits of Peer Review
text:
Peer review is the process through which scholars evaluate each other's work before a journal agrees to publish it. Although the system is widely regarded as the cornerstone of academic quality control, it has been criticised for its slowness and for the difficulty of finding reviewers who are both qualified and available. Critics also point out that reviewers may be influenced by the reputation of the authors or by whether the findings confirm their own expectations.

Nevertheless, supporters argue that the process, however imperfect, filters out weak research and encourages authors to clarify their arguments. Many journals have therefore experimented with open review, in which the reviewers' names and comments are published alongside the article. Such transparency may make reviewers more careful, although it can also discourage candid criticism.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what is peer review?
options: A process in which scholars evaluate each other's work before publication
A method for translating academic articles
A type of online survey for students
A way of counting how often articles are cited

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what have many journals experimented with?
options: Open review, in which reviewers' names and comments are published
Paid reviewers who work only on weekends
Reviews that contain no written comments

questions.text: What can be inferred from critics' concern about reviewers whose findings confirm their own expectations?
options: Reviewers may favour results that fit what they already believe
Reviewers only read the abstracts of articles
Reviewers are always paid more for positive results

questions.text: Why might open review both improve and limit the quality of feedback?
options: It removes the need for editors altogether
It makes reviewers accountable but may make them less willing to be frank
It guarantees that every article will be published
It shortens the time needed for a journal to decide

paragraph_translations: La revisión por pares es el proceso mediante el cual los académicos evalúan el trabajo de otros antes de que una revista acepte publicarlo. Aunque el sistema es ampliamente considerado la piedra angular del control de calidad académico, ha sido criticado por su lentitud y por la dificultad de encontrar revisores que sean a la vez calificados y disponibles. Los críticos también señalan que los revisores pueden verse influidos por la reputación de los autores o por si los resultados confirman sus propias expectativas.

Sin embargo, quienes defienden el sistema sostienen que el proceso, por imperfecto que sea, filtra las investigaciones débiles y anima a los autores a aclarar sus argumentos. Por ello, muchas revistas han experimentado con la revisión abierta, en la que los nombres y comentarios de los revisores se publican junto con el artículo. Esta transparencia puede hacer que los revisores sean más cuidadosos, aunque también puede desalentar las críticas francas.
